cur:manuscripts-valcavado-christ-angel-j.summary: At the top, Christ sits enthroned in a starry medallion between two angels; in the middle register John falls at the feet of the angel, who forbids him to worship him; below, John stands with his book before the seven churches. The page closes the Apocalypse cycle with the words 'I Jesus have sent mine angel'.
facts: The Valcavado Beatus was written and illuminated in 970 by the monk Oveco for Abbot Sempronius of Valcavado, in the reign of Ramiro III of León; it has 230 surviving leaves and 87 miniatures.
After the expulsion of the Jesuits under Charles III, the manuscript passed from their college of San Ambrosio in Valladolid to the University of Valladolid.

yuag:57878.summary: Cut into a tiny oval of carnelian, a standing shepherd carries a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs at his chest, while small animals stand at his feet. Such engraved gems were set in rings and used as seals, so the image would have been pressed into wax by its owner. In Christian hands the old pastoral motif became an image of Christ the Good Shepherd, though on a gem without Christian symbols the meaning cannot be certain.
facts: The gem is only about 1.5 cm high; Yale describes it as Roman work from Syria of the 3rd–4th century.
The ram-bearer (kriophoros) figure goes back to Greek art, where it was associated with Hermes, and was adapted by Christians as an image of Christ the Good Shepherd.
It was given to the Yale University Art Gallery in 1986 by Ambassador and Mrs William L. Eagleton, Jr.
yuag:57878.notes: Identification uncertain: shepherds carrying sheep appear on both pagan and Christian gems, and this one shows no Christian symbol; the museum's title calls it a Good Shepherd.
